To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rates of readmission and mortality for heart failure in the four racial/ethnic populations studied differed, even after controlling for important clinical, hospital, socioeconomic and other factors, and that the differences in the rate of readmission for heart failure between the white and Hispanic populations disappeared when the model included information on socioeconomic status.

among Medicare patients hospitalized with heart failure, short‐ and longer‐term readmission and mortality differed among 4 major race/ethnic populations and that the differences persisted even after controlling clinical, hospital, socioeconomic, and other factors.
among Medicare patients hospitalized with heart failure (HF), short‐term (30‐day) and long‐term (1‐year) readmission rates and survival varied by race/ethnicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of race and ethnicity on outcomes in heart failure.
the impact of race/ethnicity on outcomes following hospitalization with heart failure (HF).
the effects of the social environment on health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the outcomes for heart failure in the 4 major ethnic groups are similar.

racial disparities in outcomes for heart failure are not eliminated by controlling for clinical, social and socioeconomic status variables and that there is a need to develop strategies to address these disparities.
the racial and ethnic differences in the readmission rate and mortality rate of patients with heart failure are not fully explained by the socioeconomic status of the patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
racial and ethnic differences in short‐ and longterm rehospitalization and death rates following HF hospitalization are largely independent of socioeconomic status and other clinical factors.

the outcomes following hospitalization of HF patients vary among different racial/ethnic groups and that these variations are not fully accounted by clinical, hospital, or socioeconomic characteristics.
the racial/ethnic differences we observed in outcomes following HF hospitalization persisted after controlling for clinical characteristics, hospital characteristics, and socioeconomic status.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the differences in outcomes between racial/ ethnic groups persisted even after controlling clinical and hospital variables, as well as socioeconomic status variables.
the differences in outcomes among racial/ethnic populations are not entirely explained by socioeconomic factors.
racial and ethnic differences in outcomes following hospitalization persist after controlling for a wide variety of patient, hospital, and community characteristics.
